source: Vul and Pashler (2008) Measuring the crowd within: probabilistic representations within individuals
finding: Averaging two guesses from one person beat either guess alone. Second guess was less accurate than the first, so the gain is not new information. A 3-week delay gave a bigger gain than an immediate second guess.
numbers: N=428, 8 CIA World Factbook percentage questions. Immediate (n=255): avg beat guess 1 t(254)=2.25 p<.05, guess 2 t(254)=6.08. Delayed (n=173): avg beat guess 1 t(172)=3.94, guess 2 t(172)=6.59. Error cut vs guess 1: 95% CI [2.5%,10.4%] immediate, [11.6%,20.4%] delayed. Worth of 2nd same-person guess = 1.11 people immediate (lambda=0.11), 1.32 people delayed (lambda=0.32).
quote: you can gain about 1/10th as much from asking yourself the same question twice as you can from getting a second opinion
limits: Short report, one task type (percent estimates), web sample. Delay-vs-immediate t(426)=2.12 was later corrected by the authors to t(426)=2.68, p=.008 (see Steegen 2014). Authors explain delay as less anchoring.
agent_relevance: Gold-standard size of the effect: a second sample from one source is worth about 0.1 to 0.3 of an independent source. Immediate resampling is the weak case; this matches G4 (samples from one model are not independent).

source: Steegen, Dewitte, Tuerlinckx, Vanpaemel (2014) Measuring the crowd within again: a pre-registered replication study
finding: High-powered pre-registered replication of Vul and Pashler. The effect replicated in both immediate and 3-week-delay conditions, with effect sizes at or above the original.
numbers: Immediate N=471 students: MSE guess1 589, guess2 615, average 541; dz=0.40 [0.31,0.49] vs guess 1, dz=0.47 [0.38,0.57] vs guess 2. Delayed N=140: MSE 517, 589, 467; dz=0.34 [0.17,0.51] vs guess 1, dz=0.72 [0.53,0.90] vs guess 2. Guess 2 was worse than guess 1 in both (immediate dz=-0.10, delayed dz=-0.25).
limits: Delay benefit was mixed: vs guess 1 the immediate-vs-delayed difference was NOT significant (gain 50 vs 48, t(609)=0.18); vs guess 2 it was (121 vs 73, d=0.30, p=.002). Original data showed the opposite pattern. Delayed condition lost many participants (21 defocused the window). Student sample.
agent_relevance: The basic effect is real and robust; the claim that delay always helps is shaky. For us: expect a small, reliable gain from a second sample, and do not count on a big delay or spacing bonus.

source: Steegen et al. (2014), literature summary of earlier replication attempts of the immediate condition
finding: Before 2014 there were four attempts at the immediate condition with mixed results. Two found a gain (Hourihan and Benjamin 2010; Rauhut and Lorenz 2011). Herzog and Hertwig (2009) found a gain whose 95% CI included zero. One unpublished attempt (Banker and McCoy) found no significant gain.
numbers: Herzog and Hertwig control condition gain: mean 0.3 percentage points, SD 2.3, median 0%, CI [0.0,0.8], d=0.12. No replication of the delayed condition existed before Steegen.
limits: Secondhand account of the unpublished failure; gain metrics differed across studies so numbers are not comparable.
agent_relevance: The honest summary is: effect exists but is small and sometimes not distinguishable from zero in a single study. Plan for gains near the low end.

source: Hourihan and Benjamin (2010) Smaller is better (when sampling from the crowd within): low memory-span individuals benefit more from multiple opportunities for estimation
finding: Replicated the immediate gain and found a moderator: people with low working-memory span gained more from averaging than high-span people. Authors say smaller memory samples overlap less across two guesses.
numbers: N=170 analysed (low span n=86, high n=84). MSE guess1 502, guess2 565, average 484 (avg vs g1 t(169)=2.15 p=.03; vs g2 t(169)=7.89). Benefit vs OSPAN r=-.16 p<.05. Worth of 2nd guess in people: 1.07 low span, 1.04 high span.
limits: Read through a page summary of the PMC article. Tiny difference between groups (1.07 vs 1.04); CIs overlap; paper itself has a 1.04 vs 1.05 inconsistency. Most subjects answered immediately; 51 later in session.
agent_relevance: A better and more consistent source reduces the gain. A strong model with a sharp answer distribution may gain least from resampling.

source: Fraundorf and Benjamin (2014) Knowing the crowd within: metacognitive limits on combining multiple judgments
finding: People underuse averaging of their own two guesses. They choose first guess, second guess or the average with weak insight. Showing labels (first/second/average) raised averaging; showing only numbers pushed people to the later, worse guess.
numbers: Pooled N about 213, 12 percent questions. Pooled MSE: first 537, second 606, average 500 (avg vs first t(212)=-4.27). Choice of average: 59 percent (labels only), 43 percent (numbers only), 45 percent (both); chance 33. Accuracy picking the better of two guesses: 56-57 percent in most studies, 47 percent numbers-only. Choosing beats averaging only if accuracy exceeds about 67 percent.
limits: Read via page summary (first 100000 characters of the page). Percent questions only; students/online sample.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G5: aggregate by fixed code rule (average or vote), not by letting the model pick the better of its own samples. Self-selection among own samples runs near 56 percent, below the 67 percent needed.

source: Authors not recorded: How the wisdom of crowds, and of the crowd within, are affected by expertise (Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications, 2021)
finding: Training participants to near-expert accuracy eliminated the inner-crowd gain while the outer-crowd (different people) gain stayed. Experts give nearly the same answer every time, so variance is too small to average away.
numbers: Numerosity task (50-100 stars), MTurk. Exp 1 (n=63, no training): inner crowd variance term a=0.05 (BF10=1417), bias b=0.09; outer crowd a=0.10, b=0.045. Exp 2 (n=62, 12 practice trials with feedback; first-guess error about 5x smaller): inner a=0.005 (BF10=0.02, strong null), outer a=0.024 (BF10 about 7e14).
quote: experts give almost the same answer every time they are asked and so they should consult the outer crowd
limits: One perceptual-estimation task; training was brief; Exp 2 pre-registered, Exp 1 not. Bayesian a/t+b model fit.
agent_relevance: Key boundary condition for us: as the model becomes more accurate and its answers more peaked, resampling the same model adds almost nothing. Gains concentrate on hard items where the model is uncertain.

source: Van de Calseyde and Efendic, replication and moderator test: Disagreeing perspectives enhance inner-crowd wisdom for difficult (but not easy) questions (Psychological Science, 2025)
finding: A prior claim that a 'disagreeing friend' second guess improves the inner crowd was challenged by a maximal-random-effects reanalysis (no overall gain). Three pre-registered experiments show the truth is item-dependent: a disagreeing perspective helps on difficult questions and hurts on easy ones.
numbers: N=2,884 total (Exp 1a 1,193; 1b 1,196; Exp 2 495), 120 percent questions in 12 blocks. Bracketing: 21 percent (self 2nd guess) vs 36 percent (disagree) in 1a. Correlation of guesses r=.74 (self) vs .33 (disagree). No overall gain in 1a: -19.31 [-51.90,13.09]; small in 1b: -29.75 [-59.23,-0.59]. Difficulty x perspective interaction 1a -1.65 [-2.51,-0.78], 1b -1.42 [-2.26,-0.59], Exp 2 (pre-registered 15 easy/15 hard) -13.49 [-19.77,-7.34]. Disagree beat self on 87 percent of hard Exp 2 items vs 33 percent of easy.
limits: Difficulty defined from first-guess error after the fact in 1a/1b (pre-registered in 2). Percentage questions, US/UK Prolific sample.
agent_relevance: Forced diversity (a persona or 'argue the other side' sample) is not a free win: it hurts when the first answer is already close. Supports G1 (doubt only on a signal) and G4 (no persona voters on single-answer problems), and supports using disagreement as the trigger for extra sampling.

source: Fermian guesstimation can boost the wisdom-of-the-inner-crowd (Scientific Reports, 2024)
finding: Compared consider-the-opposite (dialectical bootstrapping), a Fermi-style decomposition second estimate, and a no-strategy control, with and without showing the first estimate. Every condition gained a little; strategy and memory aid did not differ significantly.
numbers: N=285 Prolific, 50 animal-property items (40 analysed). Share of items where average beat first guess exceeded 50 percent in all six cells; excess 2.1 to 4.3 points (d=0.20 to 0.52). Strategy effect F(2,279)=1.07 p=.345; memory aid F(1,279)=0.037 p=.847. Median error reduction Fermian 2.6 and 3.9 percent (d=0.34, 0.31); dialectical vs control d=0.007 (untrimmed) but d=0.40 p=.014 (20 percent trimmed). Bracketing helpful in 70.6 percent of cases, unhelpful 29.4 percent.
limits: Conclusions flip between trimmed and untrimmed means. Confirms White and Antonakis' point that results depend on trimming. Animal facts only.
agent_relevance: Gains from clever second-sample strategies are a few percent and fragile to the metric. A third of forced 'other side' samples overshoot and hurt; a code-side robust aggregator (median or trimmed) is safer than a plain mean.

source: Fujisaki, Yang, Ueda (2023) On an effective and efficient method for exploiting the wisdom of the inner crowd (Scientific Reports)
finding: Asking people for their own estimate, then their estimate of public opinion, and averaging gave a larger gain than dialectical bootstrapping or plain repeated guessing, and took no more time than repeated guessing. Gain was larger when participants were confident in the first answer. Five estimates gave no more gain than two.
numbers: Exp 1 n=150 Other's-perspective: 62.0 percent of people improved (93/150), chi2=9.07 p=.0026; Exp 2 n=28: 85.7 percent improved. MSE reduction 95% CI Exp 1: other-perspective [29.40,75.63], dialectical [19.69,68.92], repeated [-1.46,33.70]; Exp 2: [57.66,136.18], [-5.57,51.47], [20.00,63.72]. Response time for 2nd estimate: dialectical [14.04,22.99] s vs other [8.94,12.28] s. Exp 3 (five estimates) gain 95% CI [47.20,126.91], no different from two (t57=0.032 p=.97).
limits: Japanese students, 8 to 20 percent questions, small Exp 2. Method contrasts partly marginal (Exp 1 other vs repeated p=.059; other vs dialectical n.s.).
agent_relevance: A cheap perspective-shift second sample beats a long rebuttal prompt. But more samples did not help, matching the hyperbolic ceiling: gain flattens after sample 2.

source: Yang and Ueda et al. (2025) An ensemble method utilising multiple thinking styles that boosts the wisdom-of-inner-crowd effect (Scientific Reports)
finding: Five estimates made with five different thinking styles (intuition, deliberation, dialectic, general-crowd view, disagreeing-other view, with a 30 minute gap) kept improving as estimates were added. Five plain repeated guesses stayed flat. Even so the five-style average was worth only about 1.5 people.
numbers: N=76 (38 per condition). Ensemble average of 5 beat repeated-condition average of 5: t=2.51 p=.012 d=0.59; beat repeated first estimate: t=2.19 p=.029 d=0.54. Hyperbola fit: worth 1.51 people at T=5; even with infinite estimates the value could not exceed 2 people. Page trend test: MSE falls monotonically with n in ensemble (z=-5.15), flat in repeated (z=1.09 p=.28).
limits: Small sample, hypothetical rewards, 30-minute gap only in ensemble arm (confound noted by authors). Fixed order of styles. Notes that earlier work (Rauhut and Lorenz 2011; Fujisaki 2023) found five plain repeats no better than two.
agent_relevance: Best human evidence that heterogeneous prompts (different methods) beat repeated identical prompts, but with a hard ceiling near 1.5 to 2 independent sources. Fits our schema: use different operators, not the same prompt many times.

source: Van Dolder and van den Assem (2018) The wisdom of the inner crowd in three large natural experiments (Nature Human Behaviour)
finding: Largest field test: within-person aggregation improves accuracy, more so with a time delay, but the benefit is tiny compared with between-person aggregation. The average of a large number of judgments from one person is barely better than the average of two judgments from two different people.
numbers: 1.2 million observations from three incentivized guessing competitions (abstract only; per-study numbers not read).
quote: the average of a large number of judgements from the same person is barely better than the average of two judgements from different people
limits: Only the abstract was read (Europe PMC). Quantity-estimation contests with prize incentives; people knew they were in a contest.
agent_relevance: Upper bound for resampling one source: infinite samples from one mind approach roughly 2 independent sources. Do not scale up N from one model and expect crowd-like accuracy.

source: Herzog and Hertwig (2009) The wisdom of many in one mind: improving individual judgments with dialectical bootstrapping (Psychological Science)
finding: Proposed dialectical bootstrapping: assume your first estimate is wrong, list reasons, give a second estimate, then average. Claimed a larger gain than just asking again, and showed benefits go beyond reliability gains. Derived conditions under which it works.
numbers: Abstract only read; no numbers from the paper itself. Secondary figure: control-condition gain d=0.12, CI including 0 (reported in Steegen 2014).
limits: Abstract only. Second estimate was shown the first (memory aid) in the strategy arm but not in the control arm, a confound later tested in b08 (memory aid had no effect, p=.847). Contested by White and Antonakis (2013) on metric and trimming; authors replied (2013).
agent_relevance: The original basis for 'consider the opposite' prompts. Later data show its edge over plain repeated guessing is small and metric-dependent.

source: White and Antonakis (2013) Quantifying accuracy improvement in sets of pooled judgments: does dialectical bootstrapping work? and Herzog and Hertwig (2013) reply
finding: A reanalysis of Herzog and Hertwig data with the same accuracy measure and four new ones could not exactly reproduce the dialectical-bootstrapping benefit and reached different conclusions on the new measures. Herzog and Hertwig replied that the measures and trimming explain the gap.
numbers: No numbers read. Description taken from the Fermian-guesstimation paper (b08), which says the discrepancy may come from 20 percent participant-trimming used by H&H but not by W&A.
limits: Abstracts empty in index; characterisation is secondhand from b08. Not opened.
agent_relevance: Warns that reported inner-crowd gains depend on metric and outlier handling. Our measurement should state the metric up front and test with and without trimming.

source: Herzog and Hertwig (2014) Think twice and then: combining or choosing in dialectical bootstrapping? (JEP: LMC)
finding: People combine their two estimates more when told to contradict themselves, and more when the two estimates disagree more. When people chose instead of combining, they did not beat the average of their crowd within.
numbers: None read (abstract only).
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Same message as Fraundorf and Benjamin: pick-the-best among own samples does not beat averaging. Combine by rule.

source: Litvinova, Herzog, Kall, Hertwig (2019/2020) How the wisdom of the inner crowd can boost accuracy of confidence judgments (preprint)
finding: For confidence ratings, averaging two confidence judgments from one person improves them on every item type. Taking the higher of the two (maximizing) only wins when items are answered correctly about 50 to 60 percent of the time or more.
numbers: Abstract only: effect sizes of averaging over maximizing d=0.67 to 1.44 in three datasets; median correlation between a person's own confidence judgments .50 to .85.
limits: Abstract only. Two-alternative choice tasks.
agent_relevance: Confidence from repeated samples: average, do not take the max. Sampled self-confidence is highly redundant (r .5 to .85).

source: Wang et al. (2022/2023) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning in language models
finding: Sampling 40 reasoning paths from one model and taking the majority answer beat greedy chain-of-thought across tasks. The gain grew with model scale in the paper's range. This is the LLM version of the crowd within, with a vote instead of an average.
numbers: 40 samples per item, averaged over 10 runs. PaLM-540B: GSM8K 56.5 to 74.4 (+17.9), AQuA 35.8 to 48.3 (+12.5), SVAMP 79.0 to 86.6 (+7.6), ASDiv 74.0 to 81.9 (+7.9), AddSub 91.9 to 93.7 (+1.8). UL2-20B: GSM8K 4.1 to 7.3 (+3.2). LaMDA-137B GSM8K 17.1 to 27.7. Abstract also: StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-c +3.9. Consistency of the vote correlates with accuracy.
limits: Gain is far larger than in the human literature, but the task is different (discrete answer, majority vote, multi-step reasoning that varies in path). Gains shrink where the baseline is near ceiling (AddSub +1.8). Old models; reasoning tasks only.
agent_relevance: For answers that can be checked by exact match, vote over diverse reasoning paths gives large gains, so the human 'small gain' prior is too pessimistic for reasoning. The vote's agreement is also a usable uncertainty signal for our impasse detector.

source: Li et al. (2024) More agents is all you need (Agent Forest, TMLR)
finding: Majority vote over many samples from the same LLM keeps raising accuracy with ensemble size across tasks. The relative gain is larger for harder tasks and weaker models.
numbers: Ensemble size 40 vs single query. GSM8K: Llama2-13B 0.35 to 0.59, GPT-3.5 0.73 to 0.85. MATH: Llama2-13B 0.03 to 0.09, GPT-3.5 0.29 to 0.39. Chess: 0.14 to 0.18 (13B), 0.51 to 0.55 (GPT-3.5). MMLU: 0.42 to 0.51 (13B), 0.59 to 0.70 (GPT-3.5). HumanEval: 0.14 to 0.18, 0.67 to 0.73. Relative gain: GSM8K easy 69 percent (13B), 37 (70B), 16 (GPT-3.5); MATH hard 200, 120, 34. Llama2-13B at 15 samples (59 percent GSM8K) matched Llama2-70B single (54 percent).
limits: Task difficulty confounded with model; accuracy curves rise then flatten; costs 40x. Chess gain only 1 to 4 points. Single-answer tasks with a clear vote.
agent_relevance: Resampling pays most when the single-shot model is weak on the item, and little when it is near ceiling or when the answer space is wide (chess). Matches the expertise boundary in b06. A small model can buy a mid-size model's accuracy with about 15 samples.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet (ICLR)
finding: Asking a model to review and revise its own answer without outside feedback does not help and often hurts. At equal numbers of responses, self-consistency beats multi-agent debate. The apparent gains from self-correction came from using oracle labels.
numbers: GPT-3.5 intrinsic self-correction by round (1, 3, 5 calls): GSM8K 75.9, 75.1, 74.7; CommonSenseQA 75.8, 38.1, 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0, 25.0, 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5, 91.5, 89.0. With oracle labels GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3 and GPT-4 95.5 to 97.5. Equal-budget table on GSM8K: 1 response 76.7; self-consistency 3 responses 82.5, 6 responses 85.3, 9 responses 88.2. Paper says debate is no better than self-consistency at equal response count. GPT-3.5 kept its initial GSM8K answer 74.7 percent of the time and was more likely to flip right to wrong than wrong to right.
limits: Table layout in the PDF text was scrambled, so individual debate cells were not read reliably; rely on the paper's stated conclusion for debate. Reasoning benchmarks, GPT-3.5/GPT-4 era.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G2/G5: an independent second sample voted in code beats a second look by the same model. The 'dialectical second guess' that works for people (reconsider) does not carry over when the model judges itself.

source: Kim, Garg, Peng, Garg (2025) Correlated errors in large language models (ICML)
finding: LLM errors are highly correlated across models. More accurate and larger models are more correlated with each other, even across providers and architectures. Same-provider models are more correlated still. The authors name within-model sampling diversity as a separate concern and say mixing models is not a panacea.
numbers: 349 models on a HuggingFace MMLU leaderboard set (12,032 questions), 71 models on Helm (14,042 questions), 20 on resume screening (1,800 pairs). When both models are wrong they agree about 60 percent on Helm (random baseline 1/3); mean pair agreement 0.423 on HuggingFace. One model pair agreed on 0.9987 of the questions both got wrong. LLM judges inflate accuracy of weaker models, due to shared errors.
limits: Multiple-choice MMLU plus one hiring task; measures between-model, not within-model, correlation. Within-model resample correlation is not reported here.
agent_relevance: If different models share about 60 percent of their wrong answers, repeated samples of one model share more. Aggregation gains are capped by shared errors; a same-model judge cannot repair them (G4, G5).

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd: LLM ensemble prediction capabilities rival human crowd accuracy
finding: Median of 12 different LLMs (3 queries each) matched a human crowd of 925 forecasters on 31 binary questions, but the best single model was as good as or better than the crowd. Shows crowd aggregation of models, not of one model.
numbers: Brier (lower better): LLM-crowd median 0.20 (SD 0.12), human crowd 0.19 (SD 0.19), p=.85; equivalence within 0.081 Brier at d=0.5. Single models: GPT-4 0.15, GPT-4 with Bing 0.16, Bard 0.19, Claude 2 0.21, Falcon-180B 0.21, Llama-2-70B 0.25, Coral 0.38. Predicting 50 percent gives 0.25. Study 2: showing the median human forecast improved GPT-4 and Claude 2 accuracy by 17 to 28 percent; simple averaging of human and machine forecasts did better still. Acquiescence bias: mean model forecast well above 50 percent.
limits: 31 questions, one three-month window, default web-interface temperatures, wide equivalence bounds. Model crowd median did not beat the best member.
agent_relevance: Between-model diversity is a different thing from our single-model case. The best-member beating the crowd shows crowd averaging is not guaranteed to beat a strong source. Acquiescence bias is shared across models (a correlated error that averaging cannot remove).

source: Halawi, Zhang, Wang, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: Aggregating a small set of sampled forecasts from the same system cut Brier score only slightly. A trimmed mean worked best; a model-based aggregation (universal self-consistency) gave no gain. The system nears but does not beat the human crowd; averaging system and crowd is best.
numbers: Validation set, 6 base reasonings per question: baseline (no ensemble) Brier 0.1676; mean 0.1656; median 0.1651; geometric mean 0.1655; trimmed mean 0.1649 (gain 0.0027, about 1.6 percent relative); USC 0.1691 (worse than baseline); human crowd 0.1600. Full test set: system about 0.179 vs crowd 0.149 (row reading from scrambled table); GPT-4-1106 alone 0.208 vs crowd 0.149. Paper states averaging system and crowd is best in every setting.
limits: Gain measured on 6 forecasts per question from GPT-4-1106 prompts plus a fine-tuned GPT-4, not identical resamples. Test-table text columns were scrambled; the validation ensemble table is the reliable one.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM analogue to Vul and Pashler: averaging several samples from one system gives a gain of a couple of percent. A model asked to merge its own samples did worse than a code-side mean. Combine with an outside signal (the human crowd) for the real gain.

source: Naik et al. (2023/2024) Diversity of thought improves reasoning abilities of LLMs (DIV-SE)
finding: Ensembling answers from different prompt approaches or personas (DIV-SE) beats self-consistency that only varies the decoding sample, at the same or lower cost. Varying the method is a stronger source of independence than temperature sampling.
numbers: GPT-4 graph coloring: SC-3 18.0, SC-5 20.0, SC-7 22.0, SC-10 23.0 vs IDIV-SE 74.0 and DIV-SE 97.0. Blocksworld 4/5: SC-3 38.2, SC-10 41.2, IDIV-SE 57.0, DIV-SE 69.6. AQuA (GPT-3.5) DIV-SE 67.7, 3.23 points above majority voting; up to 14.3 points gain on AQuA/graph coloring, 16.87 on a GPT-4 benchmark vs zero-shot CoT baseline.
limits: Shown on planning and graph coloring, where plain SC is near its weakest. Prompt-diverse ensembling costs extra calls to design approaches. Benchmarks are specific; gains not guaranteed on knowledge items.
agent_relevance: The LLM counterpart of b10: different approaches, not the same prompt resampled. Supports giving the loop distinct operators rather than repeated identical drafts. Still conflicts with G4 on persona voters for single-answer problems; the evidence here is for method diversity, test before adopting.

source: Mixed summary: failure of added samples in human work (Rauhut and Lorenz 2011, as reported by Yang et al. 2025)
finding: Rauhut and Lorenz let people make five plain estimates of the same quantity. Averaging five was no more accurate than averaging the first two. The authors of b10 say no fix was found for over a decade.
numbers: No figures from the original (not opened). Fujisaki et al. also found their five-estimate perspective variant no better than two (b09, t57=0.032).
limits: Secondhand, from the 2025 paper's introduction and discussion. Original Rauhut and Lorenz 2011 (J Math Psych) not read.
agent_relevance: The hyperbolic ceiling: after the second sample the marginal gain is near zero for identical prompts. Cap plain resampling at a small N.

source: Synthesis of moderators across opened human studies
finding: Gains grow with (1) more independence between samples (delay, different method, other perspective), (2) harder items and higher first-guess error, (3) lower first-guess accuracy or lower memory span. Gains shrink or vanish with (1) expertise or training that narrows the answer distribution, (2) easy items, (3) identical repeated prompts beyond two.
numbers: See b02, b04, b06, b07, b09, b10 for the figures behind each moderator.
limits: Moderators come from different tasks and mostly percent-estimation questions. Culture and time pressure were not tested in any source I opened.
agent_relevance: Operational rule for the agent: spend extra samples only when the first answer is uncertain or checks fail; vary method rather than re-asking; expect about 1.1 to 1.5 independent sources worth, not N.

source: Diversity prediction theorem as applied to the inner crowd (Page 2007, as used in b06 and b10)
finding: Collective error equals average individual error minus the diversity (variance) of the estimates. Averaging helps exactly by the spread of the samples. A set of near-identical samples gains nothing even if each is good.
numbers: Toy example in b06: crowd A (variance 116.22) vs crowd B (variance 1.56) with the same bias 0.11; MSE 116.33 vs 1.67. In b10 the ensemble condition had worse per-estimate error but higher diversity and so a lower collective error than repeated guessing.
limits: Theorem is an identity, not a causal claim; it says nothing about whether the diversity is informative (a wild guess adds variance but harms the average, b07).
agent_relevance: Gives the check we can run in code: measure spread of samples before paying for more; zero spread means stop. Useful and cheap diversity signal for the impasse detector.

source: Wang et al. 2022 (self-consistency), scale and sampling robustness section
finding: Self-consistency gain held across sampling settings and model scales. The agreement of the winning answer tracked accuracy. Gains were larger for bigger models in the range tested and smaller where the baseline was near ceiling.
numbers: UL2-20B gains +3 to +6 points; LaMDA-137B and GPT-3 +9 to +23; PaLM-540B and GPT-3 +12 to +18 on AQuA and GSM8K, +7 to +11 on SVAMP and ASDiv. Zero-shot CoT on GSM8K reported +26.2 points. With imperfect prompts greedy fell 17.1 to 14.9 and self-consistency recovered the loss.
limits: Gains are against greedy chain-of-thought, a weak single-sample baseline. Older models.
agent_relevance: Baseline choice matters: compare to a single sampled answer at working settings, not greedy, or the gain looks bigger. Agreement rate is a usable confidence signal for our gating.
